items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the civil rights law and the executive law, in relation to
prohibiting discrimination by public utility companies; and to amend the
public service law, in relation to emergency planning and response
items.lawCode: Amd §42, Civ Rts L; amd §296, Exec L; amd §66, add §66-p, Pub Serv L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7262

SPONSOR: MURPHY
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the civil rights law and the executive
law, in relation to prohibiting discrimination by public utility compa-
nies; and to amend the public service law, in relation to emergency
planning and response

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Prohibits public utilities from discriminating on the basis of age,
gender, sexual orientation, military or veteran status, or union member-
ship in the delivery of services.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill prohibits discrimination by utility companies by
expanding the definition of unlawful discrimination to include refusal
to provide service to, or provide employment to any person on the basis
of age, gender, sexual orientation, military, veteran or disabled veter-
an status, union membership, race, creed, color or national origin.

Section two of the bill provides that violations of section forty-two of
the civil rights law shall be considered an unlawful discriminatory
practice.

Section three of the bill strengthens the requirements for emergency
plans that are filed annually with the public service commission by
requiring they include:

*Means for prohibiting unlawful discrimination during the restoration of
service;

*Procedures to be followed for accurately determining the extent of an
outage, the location of affected areas and the estimated number of
customers affected;

*Procedures for estimating the time required for the restoration of
service and communicating such times to the public;

*Policies for initiating and implementing load relief and load control
programs; and

*Procedures for obtaining and distributing dry ice.

Section three of the bill further requires that the emergency plans be
filed annually, and certified with the public service commission, along
with the opportunity for public comment. As part of its review, the
commission shall review the adequacy of any policies for reimbursing
customers for losses due to outages and inadvertent or intentional
shutoffs of electricity. Section three also provides that within sixty
days of the restoration of service following an incident where the
restoration period exceeds forty-eight hours, the commission may imme-
diately order any modifications or conditions to the corporation's emer-
gency plan it deems necessary.

Section four of the bill authorizes the public service commission to
establish performance benchmarks and standards for utility companies
which their emergency plans must meet. The benchmarks and standards
shall address power outages which affect more than ten percent of a
utility companies' customers for more than forty-eight hours, or any
number of customers who suffer forty-eight hours of aggregate power loss
within any fourteen day period. The benchmarks shall include:

*The means of preventing unlawful discrimination during an outage;

*Minimum staffing and equipment levels to serve customers in the event
of an outage;

*Timetables for the restoration of outages;

*Creation of a communication plan between each company and customers,
including periods that are not during normal business hours;

*Mutual aid agreements with other utilities;

*Notification of relevant state, municipal and/or emergency operations
center officials concerning emergency preparation, road clearing and the
establishment of restoration priorities;

*Tree trimming and measures to reduce outages caused by trees and limbs;
and

*Reimbursement to residential customers for loss of food, prescription
drugs, and other perishables during an outage following proof of loss

Section four further provides that the commission shall review each
company's current practices following an emergency or incident in which
more than ten percent of any such company's customers were without power
for more than forty-eight consecutive hours, or forty-eight aggregate
hours within any fourteen day period and authorizes the commission to
levy civil penalties to companies which fail to meet the commission's
benchmark standards in an amount not to exceed a total of two and one-
half percent of such company's gross annual revenues from electric
distribution.

Section five states the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Discrimination in any form is reprehensible. The state's antidiscrimi-
nation statutes for public utility companies are out of date and do not
adequately protect employees and consumers.  Additionally, the emergency
plans utility companies are required to file do not address the means by
which the companies shall prevent unlawful discriminatory practices
during the restoration of service.  Even years after Hurricane Sandy,
Hurricane Irene, and the October Nor'easter, many consumers feel that
emergency plan requirements are still inadequate. Meanwhile, while the
Public Service Commission is required to set forth areas which emergency
plans must address, it is not required to provide for any sort of mini-
mum standards which the plans must meet. Legislation is needed to
address these issues.

This bill also addresses ongoing concerns over the definition of an
outage incident by expanding the definition to include the loss of power
due to an emergency event, and inadvertent or intentional shut-offs when
they affect more than ten percent of a utility company's customers, or
any number of customers who suffer more than forty-eight hours of aggre-
gate power loss within a two-week period.

Further, the bill requires the Public Service Commission to establish
minimum benchmarks that public utility companies must meet in order to
prevent unlawful discrimination, provide accurate estimates for restora-
tion times, communicate with the general public and elected officials
and create policies to adequately review reimbursement policies for
customers who suffer damages due to a power loss incident. It also
strengthens emergency plan requirements, creates an annual review proc-
ess and allows for public comment.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state or municipalities.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public service law, in relation to emergency planning and
response; in relation to vegetation management and communications during power
outages; and relates to the use of penalties towards investments in improving
storm restoration
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7262A             Revised 6/19/18

SPONSOR: MURPHY
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the public service law, in relation to
emergency planning and response; in relation to vegetation management
and communications during power outages; and relates to the use of
penalties towards investments in improving storm restoration

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill establishes new directives and strengthens existing directives
that utilities must follow in responding to storms and power outages,
and directs the Public Service Commission (PSC) to implement such direc-
tives, which are designed enhance communication and vegetation manage-
ment in particular. The bill also directs the PSC to study whether util-
ity storm restoration efforts are impacted by having noncontiguous
service territories.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one amends subdivision 21 of Section 66 of the public service
law to require that an electric corporation must file a yearly emergency
plan with updated internal and external contacts for persons necessary
to execute the plan and key company personnel assigned service restora-
tion responsibilities. Prior to review and approval of such plan, the
PSC must seek comments from state and local agencies, including state
office of emergency management, division of homeland security, emergency
services and other agencies that provide emergency shelter as well as
members of the public, and may require modifications or otherwise
prescribe conditions for approval. The PSC review must consider the
adequacy of any policies for reimbursing customers for losses due to
outages or inadvertent intentional shutoffs of electricity. When there
is an emergency that results in an outage in excess of seventy-two
hours, each electric corporation must submit to the PSC a review of
system restoration performance.

Section two directs the PSC to order that any penalties or settlements
against any electric corporation in connection with the winter storms
Quinn and Riley, which impacted the counties of Dutchess, Westchester,
Putnam and Sullivan, shall be used exclusively for investments by such
electric corporations to improve storm restoration through increased
resiliency and improved emergency response. Such funds must be invested
directly into the areas impacted, targeting the locations that received
the most damage from the foregoing storms. These investments would
include: communication upgrades, tree trimming costs, funding for train-
ing of emergency first responders, upgrade of pole materials to with-
stand storms, technology upgrades, including the use of drones to
increase effectiveness and time for assessment of damages, the use of
monitoring devices at critical facilities located in the impacted coun-
ties referenced herein and generators for customers with life support
assistance.

The bill directs the PSC to encourage electric corporations to identify
and disseminate best practices in emergency planning and response and
authorizes the PSC to initiate a statewide emergency preparedness and
storm management planning process involving all electric corporations
and other involved organizations. A failure to comply with any provision
of this legislation would result in judicial or a proceeding for admin-
istrative sanctions and penalties by the PSC.
Section 3 adds a new section 66-p to the PSL to ensure that electric
corporations employ a vegetation manager who is an electric utility
arborist. The PSC would promulgate regulations and define "hazard
trees", which would include trees that are diseased or otherwise create
danger to energized conductors' reliable supply of electric power. The
electric corporation shall determine if it is permitted to remove or
mitigate hazard trees and shall do so as soon as possible.  If permis-
sion is required to remove hazard trees, the electric corporation shall
reasonably attempt to obtain permission to remove or mitigate the hazard
trees as determined by the PSC.

Section 4 amends the PSL by adding section 66-q to require the PSC to
review the communication plans of each electric corporation as to the
effectiveness of the electric corporation's communication with custom-
ers, especially those with life support assistance, as well as federal,
state, municipal and emergency operations center officials during power
outages. The PSC shall make recommendations on improvements that elec-
tric corporations should make with respect to their communication poli-
cies.

Section 5 would establish a non-contiguous service territory study that
will examine whether electric corporations that operate in non-contigu-
ous service territories are able to effectively mobilize personnel,
equipment and resources to respond to storm damage in a reasonable time-
frame as compared to electric corporations with contiguous territories.
Additionally, the PSC is directed to study whether noncontiguous service
territories pose any barriers to communication with local governments.
Finally, the study shall review the mutual aid response for storms Quinn
and Riley and provide recommendations related to improving the effec-
tiveness of those mutual aid agreements.

Section 6 provides for the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Year after year, storm after storm, certain electric corporations
continue to fail the customers they serve in their response to severe
weather events, the restoration of power to their affected customers,
and their ability to accurately communicate to customers and state and
local officials regarding projections for the restoration of power.
These inadequacies force customers to seek alternative accommodations,
which can cost hundreds of dollars more than their monthly utility bill.
During a recent outage in Westchester County, an individual who was
homebound due to a medical condition was misinformed regarding the time-
frame in which power would be restored, which lead to that individual
remaining home without heat for more than 36 hours before eventually
being discovered. Providing a false sense of hope does nothing to
further the goal of advising customers on how they might choose to
manage a loss of power to their residence. Additionally, when local
officials rely on electric corporation communications during weather
emergencies, the public is often provided incomplete or inaccurate
information. Customers and local officials are kept guessing, leading to
ill-informed decision making that unnecessarily puts lives at risk.

After Super Storm Sandy and Hurricane Irene impacted New York, electric
customers were led to believe that electric corporations had absorbed
the lessons learned and were more than prepared to react to future high
impact weather events due to the partial implementation of the findings
of the Moreland Commission on Utility Storm Preparation and Response.
However, most recently during Winter Storms Quinn and Riley, many
consumers and public officials expressed dismay that emergency plan
implementation remained inadequate. The PSC is required to set forth
areas which emergency plans must address, however these plans need
further scrutiny with regard to the effectiveness of communication to
affected customers, federal, state, county and local municipalities.
Additionally, failure to abide by emergency preparedness plans filed
with the PSC and Orders issued by the PSC must result in greater
accountability and consequences in the form of fines and penalties
assessed on offending electric corporations as ordered by the PSC.

Under this legislation, where fines and penalties are assessed, those
dollars will be re-invested in the community to bolster infrastructure
resiliency and emergency response, focusing on the areas that were hit
the hardest. Electric corporations will be required to invest such funds
in the following: communication upgrades; tree trimming costs; funding
for training of emergency first responders; upgrade of pole materials to
withstand storms; technology upgrades, including the use of drones to
increase the effectiveness and time of damage assessments; use of moni-
toring devices at critical facilities located in the impacted counties
and generators for customers with life support assistance.

This legislation further addresses vegetation management, an issue that
was raised repeatedly at the joint public hearing held by the New York
State Senate Standing Committees on Investigations and Government Oper-
ations, Energy and. Telecommunications and Aging. This bill would
require all electric corporations to employ a vegetation manager charged
with implementing new regulations addressing the identification and
removal of hazardous trees, which are structurally unsound due to
disease or rot, or pose a danger to interruption of service when those
trees are located within or without a right-of-way.

Finally, this legislation requires the PSC to conduct a study examining
of the effectiveness of electric corporations that operate in non-conti-
guous territories when responding to storm damage, if any issues exist
that may prevent effective communication and coordination with local
governments, and assess the effectiveness of mutual aid agreements. It
is time to hold our electric providers to a higher standard, especially
when their customers are often without a choice in who they receive
service from. This legislation does just that.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state or municipalities.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

summary: Requires public utilities to submit emergency preparation plans to the public service commission on an annual basis; requires submission of reports after the restoration of service in an emergency; relates to vegetation management and communications during power outages; requires penalties to be used towards investments in improving storm restoration.
